en: It should be stated that it is the nature of that action; [this is] suspected by [the opponent] on account of earthness and so forth.

Because it would involve the conceptual complexity (*gaurava*) of postulating multiple bodies pervaded by the universal "earth-ness" (*pṛthivītva*) and so forth. Regarding the term "internal" (*ādhyātmika*):
internal air is that which is called *prāṇa*. He raises an objection with the words "in that very [instance]" (*tatraiva*).
Regarding "broken and wounded" (*bhagnakṣata*): this refers to those whose parts have been separated due to specific disjunctions caused by breaking or wounding.
"From healing and so forth"—by "and so forth," growth is included; and growth is the accumulation of constituent parts.
"From the inference thereof" means from the inference based on the connection with the internal wind (*ādhyātmikavāyu*). Now, one might object:
there is no proof that the wind which is the cause of healing broken or wounded limbs is the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
If you say this is not so, consider: "The *sarala* and *arjuna* trees growing on the banks of the Narmadā attain the supreme goal through contact with the waters of the Narmadā.
Having uttered 'huṃ' or 'tuṃ' at a teacher, or having defeated a Brahmin in debate, [one is reborn] in a cremation ground..."

"A tree grows, frequented by herons and vultures"—since scripture (*āgama*) alone is the authority in this matter. Regarding the phrase "by being a final substance" (*antyāvayavitvena*): the meaning is "by being a substance that does not originate another substance.

He says "or rather" (*athavā*) because [the definition] would lack pervasion (*avyāpti*) due to the absence of movement in a dead body; for [otherwise], the nature of a jar (*ghaṭatva*) would be included.
The term "possessing motion" (*ceṣṭāvat*) is included to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to a jar.

The term "ultimate whole" (*antyāvayavī*) is included to exclude over-extension to hands and the like. It should not be argued that "hand-ness" (*hastatva*) and so forth are not universals (*jāti*) because they would involve a confusion (*saṅkara*) with "earth-ness" (*pṛthivītva*) and other such categories.

Because [the author] accepts various properties such as *hasta-tva* (hand-ness) which are pervaded by *pṛthivī-tva* (earth-ness) and so forth, there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to jars and the like, which possess such a genus as *pṛthivī-tva*. Therefore, he states another definition: "the ultimate whole" (*antyāvayavī*). By the phrase "subsisting in the ultimate whole alone,"...

The exclusion of the genus "earth-ness" (*pṛthivītva-jāti*) [is achieved by the term "body"]. By the phrase "subsisting in that which possesses movement" (*ceṣṭāvadvṛtti*), the exclusion of pot-ness (*ghaṭatva*) and so forth is achieved. Furthermore, "movement" (*ceṣṭā*) should be understood as action for the purpose of attaining the beneficial and avoiding the harmful, and not merely as vibration (*spandana*), because [the latter] exists even in pots and the like. Now, [one might object]:...

Since the application of the definition [of genus] occurs by taking "deityhood" (*devatva*) as the genus, he says: "belonging to water," etc. Regarding the phrase "of deityhood also": the word "also" (*api*) includes "man-lion-ness" (*nṛsiṃhatva*). Regarding the phrase "due to the absence of being a genus":
the intended meaning is "due to the confusion of genera" (*jātisaṅkara*). If one were to argue that the confusion of genera is not a defect... [the response follows].

Alternatively, if one accepts that "godhood" (*devatva*), "bodiness" (*śarīratva*), and so forth are distinct universals (*jāti*), it should be understood that the definition is consistent by taking the universal of "godhood" or "bodiness" itself as the basis. Regarding the phrase "among color and the rest": taste, smell, and touch are the referents of the word "and the rest" (*ādi*). This [definition] applies to water that manifests the odor of a new jar, and to the mind (*manas*).

The particle *eva* is for the purpose of excluding deviation (*vyabhicāra*). When it is included, there is no fault, because even the juice of sugar-cane (*sakturasas*) is a manifestor [of sweetness]. To prevent the unestablished nature of the reason (*hetvaprasiddhi*)—since the olfactory organ (*ghrāṇendriya*) is a manifestor of the genus "odor-ness" (*gandhatva*)—the middle portion [of the definition] is included in the reason. Nor should it be said that a qualifier which excludes the unestablished is useless.

For, just as in the case of the cognition of deviation (*vyabhicārajñāna*), it is universally established that even when the reason (*hetu*) is unestablished (*aprasiddha*), one must employ a qualifying attribute (*viśeṣaṇa*) that excludes such non-establishment— since the cognition of pervasion (*vyāpti*) is absent [in that case]—
because that is the very purpose [of the qualification].
This is because the word "only" (*eva*) is used in conjunction with the middle term within the causal statement.

Thus, the point is that in order to avoid the fallacy of the reason being unestablished (*asiddhi*) in the case of the example—where substances such as ghee, which manifest their own color and so forth, would otherwise qualify—the qualification "belonging to another" (*parakīyatva*) must be applied to the color and other qualities. Regarding the phrase "of that": it means "of the water that manifests the odor of the new earthen vessel."

Nor should it be argued that the reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) with respect to that particular water which, while manifesting the odor of a new clay pot, does not manifest the taste of the flour-mash;
for [the reason] consists in the incapacity for the nature of a direct perception whose objects are the color and other qualities belonging to another.
Because it is intended [to be so], even in water that manifests the fragrance of a new earthen vessel, the property of being water—which is the delimitor of the manifestation of taste—is present;
this is the view of Dinakara.
He states "or else" (*yadvā*) because of the parsimony (*lāghava*) resulting from not introducing the qualifier "belonging to another" (*parakīya*). If that were not provided...

He states the reason: "brought by the wind" (*vāyūpanītā*). This is to be understood here: the intention regarding the three reasons lies in the phrase "while not manifesting color and so forth. [The reason] "while not manifesting sound, yet manifesting odor" is subject to deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of water that manifests the odor of a new earthen bowl; therefore, [the qualification is necessary].

This is because the author of the treatise had no such intention. In that context, among the reasons [adduced], the qualification "belonging to another" (*parakīyatva*) applies to color, taste, and touch.

Nor is there a fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the first reason with respect to water that manifests the odor of a new earthen jar, since that water also manifests the blue color of the faded ink-letters. Nor is there a fallacy in the third reason...
In that regard, there is a deviation (vyabhicāra) because even by way of this [objection], another alternative hypothesis is proposed;

for in that case as well, there are three reasons not incorporating the qualification "belonging to another. Among those, regarding the contact with the olfactory organ (ghrāṇendriya-sannikarṣa), "organ-ness" (indriyatva) is not a genus (jāti), because it would overlap (sāṅkarya) with "fire-ness" (tejastva) and so forth.

However, it should be understood as that which will be explained by the words "other than sound" (*śabdetara*) and so forth. Now, one might object: "Objecthood (*viṣayatva*) is not a genus (*jāti*), because it exists even in universals (*sāmānya*) and the like; therefore, he states its definition: 'The means of enjoyment' (*upabhoga*). Although being the direct means of enjoyment is [the definition], it is under-extensive (*avyāpta*) in the case of dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) and so forth.

Since the quality of being a means for experience—whether direct or indirect—is present even in the atom (*paramāṇu*), there would be a contradiction with the text stating that [the category of "means of experience"] extends from the dyad (*dvyaṇuka*) up to the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*). Nevertheless, what is intended here is the state of being a means for experience, whether direct or indirect; and the atom, too, [possesses this].

Since it is precisely the object—the earth in its state as an effect—that is divided into three types, it is shown that the object of the earth as an effect alone is [the subject] starting with "the dyad" (dvyaṇuka) and so forth; thus, there is no contradiction with that text. For this very reason, it was stated: "its enjoyment, both directly and indirectly."
Or rather, it certainly produces [the effect]. In the phrase "the collection of effects" (*kāryajātam*), the word *jāta* has entered the text by way of scribal accident.

Regarding the expression "dependent on the unseen" (*adṛṣṭādhīnam*): here, the causality of the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*) with respect to every effect does not exist through the relation of inherence (*samavāya*), because there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*); for the unseen does not exist by way of inherence in the potsherds and so forth, which are the substrata of jars and other such things. As for that which...
It is claimed that the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) is the cause of every effect through its conjunction with its own inherent substratum (*svasamavāyin*). That is not correct;

for there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of the ether (*gagana*), which is the locus of the effects sound and form, because there is no conjunction of the self—the inherent substratum of the unseen force—with the ether. Rather, its causality [in respect to those effects] is established through conjunction with that which is conjoined with its own inherent substratum (*svasamavāyisaṃyuktasaṃyoga*).
This, however, is what must be understood: the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) is not a cause with respect to the effect itself directly;

for it is never observed that when the causal totality (*sāmagrī*) has come together, there is a delay in the effect due to a delay in the unseen force, which would allow it to be a direct cause. Rather, it is so by way of bringing about the causal totality.

*The Dinakarī* [comments]: Generally, its utility occurs only through a causal chain (*paramparā*), though in some cases—such as the movement of clouds—it is a direct cause; otherwise, its status as a producer of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) would be untenable.

For this very reason, the word *adhīna* (dependent) is employed to convey the state of being produced, whether directly or through a causal chain. The meaning is: that which is dependent upon a certain unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*), or dependent upon the unseen merit of a particular person, is the effect of that [person]. Its experience...
It is the means for the experience of that puruṣa; the meaning is that it is the effect of that [puruṣa]. "Its experience" refers to the means for the experience of that puruṣa.
By this, it is meant that the effects such as dyads (dvyaṇuka) and so forth serve as the means for the experience of that respective puruṣa. Now, if this is so—

Since everything would otherwise be established merely as an object, the threefold division of earth—into body, sense organ, and object—would not be proven; therefore, he says: "Of the body and the sense organ" (verse 38).
Thus ends the section on earth. He states the proof for the genus "water-ness" (jalatva) with the words: "Oleaginousness," etc.

The sense is that, since there is no subverting evidence against the establishment of a property by virtue of its being a delimiting factor of causality (*kāraṇatāvacchedakatā*), that property possesses the nature of a universal (*jāti*). Dinakari [states]: "Although a property residing in eternal things cannot be a delimiting factor of effectness (*kāryatāvacchedakatva*), it is not possible for oiliness (*snehatva*) to be a delimiting factor of effectness. Thus he raises an objection with the words "even though" (*yadyapi*). Likewise...

The delimitant of effecthood (*kāryatāvacchedaka*). In reality, however, since there is no fault in a property common to eternal entities being the delimitant of effecthood, the word "produced" (*janya*) need not be included at all. [Objection:
But just as in the case of a staff standing in a forest and so forth—which do not bring about a result—the property that serves as the delimitant of causality...
To the objection that a genus such as "stick-ness" (daṇḍatva) might likewise exist here [in the case of the self], he says: "Of that" (tasya).

The meaning is that there is no deficiency whatsoever regarding the intrinsic fitness (svarūpayogyatā) of the stick and so forth, because, being non-eternal, it lacks the capacity to produce the result [of cognition].

"Of the genus *janya-jalatva* (the genus of produced water)" means of the genus residing solely in produced water. "Delimited by that" means delimited by the genus *janya-jalatva*. Nor should it be argued that, in this way, the property of being water (*jalatva*) would not exist in the ultimate constituent part (*antyāvayavin*) of water;
for we do not admit that water has an ultimate constituent part. Now [one might object]:...

If it is argued that "let viscidity (sneha) alone be the cause for that which is delimited by water-ness (jalatva), through the relation of inherence (samavāya), because this is simpler than the postulation of an additional universal (jāti)," we say no. For, regarding the question of whether the causality for that which is delimited by water-ness consists in being viscidity or in being cold touch (śītasparśa), [the former is preferred]. *The Dinakarī:* Regarding the statement: "Let viscidity alone be the cause for that which is delimited by water-ness, through the relation of inherence, because this is simpler than the postulation of an additional universal," we say no. For, regarding the question of whether the causality for that which is delimited by water-ness consists in being viscidity or in being cold touch, [the former is preferred]. *The Rāmarudrī:* Regarding the statement: "Let viscidity alone be the cause for that which is delimited by water-ness, through the relation of inherence, because this is simpler than the postulation of an additional universal," we say no. For, regarding the question of whether the causality for that which is delimited by water-ness consists in being viscidity or in being cold touch, [the former is preferred]. *The Bhāṣya-paricaya:* Regarding the statement: "Let viscidity alone be the cause for that which is delimited by water-ness, through the relation of inherence, because this is simpler than the postulation of an additional universal," we say no. Because there is no decisive criterion (*vinigamanā*) [to choose between alternatives], the existence of an additional universal (*jāti*) is established; for one adopts that which is already well-established (*klṛptatama*), since there is no lack of a decisive criterion regarding what must be postulated. Some, however, maintain that the causality of wet fuel (*ārdrandhana*) and so forth with respect to smoke and the like is beyond dispute, and as for this "wetness" (*ārdratva*),...

Some say that since there is no decisive evidence (*vinigamanāviraha*) as to whether the cause is "being conjoined with water" (i.e., fuel conjoined with water) or "water conjoined with fuel," the properties of "water-ness" (*jalatva*) and "fuel-ness" (*indhanatva*) must each independently serve as the delimitors of causality (*kāraṇatāvacchedaka*), thereby establishing the universal "water-ness. Others, however, [argue as follows]:

The existence of the universal *jalatva* (water-ness) as common to atoms is established by its being the delimiting property (*avacchedaka*) of the inherent causality (*samavāyikāraṇatā*) delimited by the universal *jalatva*, which is proven through the perception of water in gross masses;
for there is no defect in the identity between the delimiting property of the effect (*kāryatāvacchedaka*) and the delimiting property of the cause (*kāraṇatāvacchedaka*).

They say that there is no fault in taking "being an effect" (*kāryatā*) as the delimitor of the eternally common property (*nityasādhāraṇadharma*), because [otherwise] there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*). Regarding the phrase "but not" (*na tu*): the ellipsis is to be supplied with "because of over-extension in earth and so forth. Intending to show that there is no harm even if "possessing a white color" (*śuklarūpavatva*) were taken as the definition, he says: "Or else" (*athavā*).

The phrase "subsisting in that which possesses color" (*rūpavadvṛtti*) is included to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to air (*vāyu*), by taking the genus *vāyutva* (airness), which is pervaded by substantiality (*dravyatva*). How *vāyutva* is a genus will be explained later.

The phrase "not subsisting in that which possesses occasional fluidity" (*naimitikadravatvavadavṛtti*) is included to prevent over-extension to earth and the other elements, by taking the genus *pṛthivītva* (earthness) and so forth.

The term "directly" (*sākṣāt*) is used to exclude [properties] such as *paṭatva* (cloth-ness). Being directly pervaded by *dravyatva* (substance-ness) means merely not being pervaded by that which pervades *dravyatva*; it does not include the inclusion of being pervaded by *dravyatva* itself. This is because properties such as *rūpatva* (color-ness) are already excluded by the qualification "residing in what possesses color" (*rūpavadvṛttitva*).
Because there is no purpose in including that [fluidity] in the definition;

for even by means of fluidity alone—which is necessarily present—the exclusion of air-ness (*vāyutva*) and so forth is achieved. And thus, it is precisely because of the absence of subsistence in that which possesses fluidity [that air is excluded].

Alternatively, since it is possible to exclude [qualities such as] cloth-ness (*paṭatva*) and so forth, the qualification "directly pervaded by substanceness" (*dravyatvasākṣādvyāpya*) need not be included;

thus there is parsimony (*lāghava*). Nevertheless, because the definition involving color (*rūpa*) was stated in the root text by the passage beginning "color is white," if one were to refine the definition so that it does not include that [color], it would contradict the root text.

It should be understood that it was not formulated in that way because doing so would contradict the original [definition], as such a formulation would involve a refinement of the definition that excludes that [property], thereby resulting in a contradiction with the root text. Furthermore, this is stated on the grounds of not accepting the universal (jāti) of corporeality (mūrtatva);
therefore, there is no deficiency even if the property of being water (jalatva) is both pervaded by substantiality (dravyatva) and pervaded by corporeality.
In order to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to jars and the like by taking "being either water or a jar" as the definition, the term "universal" (*jāti*) is used.

In some versions, the reading is "subsisting in that which possesses white color" (*śuklarūpavadvṛtti*); in that case, either the word "white" (*śukla*) or the word "color" (*rūpa*) is superfluous. And it is exactly in this way that the exclusion [of other colors] occurs in the phrase "a color other than non-luminous white."
The term "substancehood directly pervaded by [the property] residing in that which possesses color" is to be understood as follows:
the phrase "not co-located with a color other than bright white" is included to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to earth (*pṛthivī*), since earthness (*pṛthivītva*) is resident in earth.
The term "other than white" is included because waterness (*jalatva*) is co-located with a white color, which would otherwise result in the fallacy of non-existence (*asaṃbhava*).

The term "tejas" (fire/heat) is used [at the beginning] to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to fire itself; furthermore, it is specified as being "only cold" even though it is not luminous. Although, according to the lexicon stating that "cold is a quality" (*guṇa*), the neuter gender would be more appropriate, nevertheless, the designation is made in the masculine because the word "touch" (*sparśa*), which is the substantive, is masculine.

In the case of "white color" (*śuklaṃ rūpam*) and so forth, it is precisely because of the neuter gender of the word *śukla*. In order to avoid over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to earth by taking the genus (*jāti*) that is earthness (*pṛthivītva*), which is pervaded by substanceness (*dravyatva*); and in order to avoid over-extension to earth by taking the genus that is bitter-earthness (*tikta-pṛthivītva*).

Regarding the phrase "tiktāvṛtti" (residing in the bitter): the remainder is to be understood according to the direction already shown. Now, one might ask: if there is an absence of blue color in water, how is blue color perceived? To this he says: "Kālindī" (the Yamunā).
The perception of blue color residing in the supporting earthly portion occurs through the relation of conjunction with its own inherent substrate.

The meaning is "in the water of the Kālindī" and so forth. "For this very reason" means: precisely because the relationship shown above is the determinant for the cognition "the water is blue. "In the sky" means:
at that time, because of the destruction of the conjunction with the jar which constitutes the aforementioned relationship. "There" means in the water. Of that...

Regarding sweetness (*mādhurya*): otherwise, as stated in the *Dinakarī*, in the absence of its being dependent on the substrate (*āśrayaupādhikatva*), the answer "because it is a manifestor" (*vyañjakatvāt*) must be supplemented by the fact that sweetness is perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) after consuming a myrobalan fruit (*harītakī*).
[The phrase] "due to the complexity of conceptualization" (*kalpanāgauravāt*) refers to [the view] that [sweetness] is not produced by the tastes of the constituent parts (*avayava-rasa*).

Since it is observed that the essence of the earth (*pṛthivīrasa*) is produced by contact with fire, if one were to accept that contact with water also produces the essence of the earth merely on the basis of this [observation], then there would be an additional causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) in the case of *harītakī*.

The sense is that there would be the fault of prolixity (gaurava) in postulating a sweet taste [in water]. Now, one might object: "Let there be a sweet taste in water; nevertheless, there is no obstacle to accepting even an acid taste, which is established by perception, in cases such as jambīra-juice. To this, he says: "of earthhood" (pṛthivītvasya).

"Because it is the delimitor of the causal capacity for producing acidity and so forth. Although it is the case that earth-ness (*pṛthivītva*) possesses the status of being a delimitor of the causal capacity for producing sweetness just as it possesses the status of being a delimitor of the causal capacity for producing acidity and so forth—and thus the two are equal—nevertheless, since sweetness is perceived even in water immediately after consuming *harītakī* and other such fruits, it is necessary to accept sweetness there; consequently, water-ness (*jalatva*) is the cause with respect to sweetness.

The meaning is that it is so conceived. Now, one might object: since sourness is perceived in the juice of a *jambīra* fruit and the like, water-ness (*jalatva*) would likewise be a cause for the perception of sour taste and other tastes; to this he says: "In the case of *jambīra* juice, etc. [The Dinakarī explains: The cognition of the sour taste residing in the *jambīra* occurs through conjunction with that which is inherent in itself (the juice), while the water residing therein...

This is the meaning. Since sourness is perceived even in a dried *jambīra* fruit, the sour taste must necessarily exist there; its perception in the water contained within it occurs through a secondary transmission (*paramparayā*). However, because the sweet taste is absent in the *harītakī*, the sweetness residing in the *harītakī* is not perceived in the water.
This is the state of affairs. It is not the case that because one experiences a bitter taste upon drinking water after eating a crab, the bitter taste must therefore exist in the water;
for the bitter taste of the crab was already perceived even before drinking the water.

Furthermore, it is established by medical science that after eating a cucumber, there is a disturbance of the bile located at the tip of the tongue, which results in the perception of its bitterness. In reality, however, it is impossible to deny the sweetness of the pure water of the Ganges experienced when drunk during the summer heat; therefore, [the taste] is sweet.

Thus, it is logical [to conclude this]. By this, it is shown that sweetness is not produced in the *harītakī* through contact with water— which would entail the fault of conceptual complexity (*kalpanāgaurava*)— but rather, a sweet taste is admitted to exist in the *harītakī* itself, just like its astringent taste, and it is simply the contact with water that manifests it, and nothing else.

[The presence] of another rasa within that [harītakī] is established by the force of the result (*phala-bala*). Furthermore, if it is argued—as Dinakara says—that because there is no evidence for a variegated rasa (*citrarasa*) as there is for a variegated color (*citrarūpa*), the harītakī is indeed devoid of rasa due to the contradiction of its constituent qualities (*guṇavirodha*), and that the perception of rasa is merely through the medium (*paramparayā*) because rasa exists in its parts; then let it be so.
The claim that contact with water is merely a manifestor of the sweetness already present in the constituent parts of the *harītakī* fruit is thus refuted.

He states another inference as proof for the genus "water-ness" (*jalatva*) with the words "In this way. Now, one might object: since coldness arises even in the absence of water-ness—as in rubbed sandalwood and the like—is there not a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) that would prevent [the inference from being valid]?

Since the causality in that case is due to its being produced water, he says "rubbed" (*ghṛṣṭa*). He establishes what was previously stated—that the touch is indeed cold—by saying "due to contact with fire" (*tejaḥsaṃyogāt*). This refers to that [water]. Furthermore, the impossibility of cooking (*pāka*) will be examined later. By the phrase "in ghee and so forth," etc., [the author indicates]...

The inclusion of oil [is for the sake of illustration]. The remainder of the sense is that "moisture (sneha) belongs to water alone" is subsequently perceived through conjunction with its own substratum; by this, moisture is excluded from ghee and the like because it exists there as an inherent property (samavāya).
As for the phrase "in water alone," no specific sub-variety of moisture is mentioned because there is no such internal distinction within it.

The delimitant of the generative power delimited by that [the former] is the delimitant of the generative power delimited by the property of natural fluidity (*sāṃsiddhikadravatvatva*). That very thing is the state of being produced water (*janyajalatva*). The point is that the delimitant of the generative power delimited by that [the latter] is the property of water (*jalatva*).

Now, if it is asked: "In this manner, since there is a difference between the two instances of *jalatva*—the first being excluded from atoms and the second being common to atoms—is the non-apprehension of that difference due to anything? [The answer is: "Because they reside in individual instances (*vyakti*) that are equally pervasive (*samaniyata*) and capable of being perceived (*yogya*). The same applies hereafter.

By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in the phrase "in oil, etc.," milk is included, but not clarified butter (*ghṛta*), because in the latter case, occasional fluidity (*naimittikadravatva*) exists by way of inherence (*samavāya*). Immediately after the word "fluidity" (*dravatva*), the remainder of the sentence is:
"it is perceived through conjunction with its own substratum. Now, [one might object]: what of the presence of wateriness (*jalatva*) in oil?
One might object that water, being contrary to fire, would not possess the quality of being conducive to burning even when mixed with oil; therefore, he says:

"by the excellence of its viscidity. The meaning is that water possessing an excellence of viscidity is indeed conducive to burning, whereas it is only that which lacks such excellence which is contrary to fire. Thus.

"He will state" — the remainder of the sense is "on the occasion of defining moisture. Regarding "as in the first case," he says with the intention that the suffix *vat* is applied to a word in the genitive case: "the meaning is 'like the earth,'" and likewise later, "the watery body," which is supported by the constituent parts of earth.
This is what must be understood. Therefore, there is no deficiency even if the arrangement of hands, feet, and so forth is impossible in mere water.
[Objection: But there is a lack of evidence for such a body, because it is not perceived.
To this he says: "In the world of Varuṇa. The sense is that the Śruti itself is the authority in that regard.
"Gandheti" [means] "in the mind which manifests taste. "Ie2> Dinakarī": To exclude deviation (vyabhicāra), it says "not manifesting smell and so forth. "Kāsāraḥ" means a lake.
In the phrase "karakādi," by the word "ādi" (and so forth), things such as wells are included. "Kaṭhinatvāt" means "because of solidity."
The meaning is "because it possesses a solid touch. Regarding the phrase "of that which has melted": the genitive case is used in the sense of the locative.

There is a reading in some places as "vilīnayoh" (in the two melted [substances]), but that is straightforward. The intended sense is that "meltedness," being of the nature of fluidity, serves as the indicator of the property of water (*jalatva*). Now, as for this "meltedness"—

It has been stated that fluidity is merely occasional (naimittika), induced by heat; and that [occasional fluidity] is not the manifester of the universal water-ness (*jalatva*). Even if the phrase "when it has melted" (*vilīne tasmin*) were interpreted to mean "when it is desired," nevertheless, because another substance arises after the destruction of the hailstone (*karakā*) and so forth, fluidity and water-ness would reside in that very [new substance].
It is not perceived in the hailstone because it has perished; therefore, he says: "whatever substance...

The point is this: since the property of being water (*jalatva*) is established by perception in another substance produced upon the destruction of the hailstone and so forth, the existence of *jalatva* in hailstones and the like is established by the aforementioned pervasion (*vyāpti*). Now, [an objection is raised] regarding snow and hailstones...

To the question, "In the absence of earthiness (*pārthivatva*), how can there be the cognition of hardness? he says: "By a particular unseen force (*adṛṣṭaviśeṣa*). Thus ends the section on water. Regarding the phrase "and thus": the meaning is, "once the universal of heat (*uṣṇatvajāti*) has been established. Now, how is this so?
In things distinct from the inherent cause of the produced sensation of heat.
